# Workbench 48–78 — Vehicle Build Configurator

An interactive, local-first web platform for visualising and configuring custom builds of
American classics, muscle cars and trucks (model years 1948–1978): pick a vehicle, inspect it
in real-time 3D, customise paint/wheels/stance/components, and plan fabrication work through
the **Titanforge** workflow.

The bundled, fully component-mapped vehicle is the **Titanforge TF-100 Stepside** — an
**original, stylised demo design generated by this project (CC0)**, not a model of any real
production vehicle. Other catalogue entries are browsable metadata only until rights-safe
assets are added. The catalogue is representative, not historically complete.

## 1970 Chevrolet Nova SS 396 (licensed asset — file not committed)

The catalogue also includes a fully mapped **1970 Nova SS 396** built from a purchased stock
3D model (115 named meshes: body panels, brightwork, lights, interior, badges and a factory
wheel set). Its Standard License does **not** permit public redistribution of the source
asset, so the model file is intentionally excluded from this repository (`.gitignore`).

To enable it locally, place the purchased GLB at:

```
public/assets/vehicles/nova-1970.glb
```

Until the file is present, the Nova shows a truthful missing-asset state in the viewer.
While its **factory wheel & tyre set** part is installed (the default), the parametric
wheel/tyre/stance system is suspended so the two never render on top of each other — remove
the factory set from the Wheels tab or Parts tab to configure wheels and stance. Left/right
panel pairs are merged in the source model, so they edit as pairs.

Nova-specific configurator features:

- **Independent paint zones**: Body, Hood, Front bumper, Rear bumper, Grille, Trim
  mouldings and Interior each take their own colour/finish (bumpers, grille and trim
  default to a chrome look but accept any paint).
- **Interchange parts** (project-original CC0 geometry in `nova-addons.glb`, generated by
  `npm run generate:nova-addons`): cowl-induction scoops (2" / 4"), a chin spoiler, and
  trunk spoilers (ducktail / wing) — installed from the Parts tab, uninstalled by default.
- **Imported wheels**: import a wheel GLB/STL via the Import dialog and tick "wheel model";
  it then appears under Wheels & Tyres and is auto-oriented and scaled to the configured
  overall tyre diameter (a display fit — not an engineering fit).
- **Custom numberplate**: the Paint tab has a Numberplate section — your text (up to 10
  characters) rendered onto generated front & rear plates in four generic colourways,
  replacing the model's baked plates. Purely decorative; remove via the "Licence plates"
  part. Driven by `plateMounts` in the asset manifest, so any vehicle can opt in.

### UV-mapped variant

The seller's UV-mapped update ships as OBJ/FBX/MAX (no glTF). Convert it with:

```
node scripts/convert-nova-uv-to-glb.mjs <dir-with-extracted-obj-and-mtl>
```

This produces `public/assets/vehicles/nova-1970-uv.glb` (also gitignored — same licence):
metres/Y-up/nose-+Z like the original, vertex-welded, Phong→PBR converted, UVs verified on
every node except the two `396` badge scripts. Node names are identical to the original
asset plus `Object001`/`Object002` (window glass split during the UV work). It is staged
for upcoming texture features (numberplates, stripes/liveries, patina); to use it as the
runtime asset today, copy it over `nova-1970.glb`.

## Setup

```bash
npm install
npm run dev            # http://localhost:5173
```

| Command | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `npm run dev` | Vite dev server |
| `npm run build` | Type-check + production build (`dist/`) |
| `npm run preview` | Serve the production build |
| `npm test` | Vitest unit + component tests (jsdom, fake-indexeddb) |
| `npm run test:e2e` | Playwright end-to-end tests (set `PW_CHROMIUM_PATH` to use a system Chromium) |
| `npm run lint` / `npm run format` | ESLint / Prettier checks |
| `npm run typecheck` | `tsc -b` with strict settings |
| `npm run generate:demo-vehicle` | Regenerate `public/assets/vehicles/tf100-stepside.glb` |

## Stack

React 19 + TypeScript (strict) + Vite 6 · Three.js r176 via React Three Fiber 9 / Drei 10 ·
Zustand 5 (custom undo/redo history) · Zod 3 schemas · Tailwind CSS 4 · IndexedDB (`idb`) ·
Vitest 3 · Playwright.

## Architecture

Configuration logic, rendering and UI are separate layers:

```
src/
  lib/            pure logic — no React, no three.js UI coupling
    schemas/      Zod schemas: Vehicle, AssetManifest, Part, PartVariant, Build,
                  FabricationRecord (+ runtime validation at import boundaries)
    catalog/      seed data: vehicles, TF-100 manifest, parts/variants, paint palettes
    build/        default build factory, stance/wheel presets
    fitment/      tyre math + indicative interference warnings; part compatibility rules
    persistence/  repository interfaces + IndexedDB implementation + autosave
    titanforge/   status metadata, adapter seam, JSON/CSV manifest export
    importing/    signature-based file validation (never trusts extension/MIME)
    export/       build JSON files, printable summary HTML
  state/          Zustand stores: build (with undo/redo history) and UI state
  three/          viewport: GLB loading, material zones, selection, ghost/isolate/
                  explode, stance rig, procedural wheels, camera presets, snapshots
  components/     panels, tabs, dialogs, trays (all data-driven)
scripts/          demo-vehicle GLB generator (node)
docs/examples/    example asset manifest + example Titanforge export
```

**Everything the UI edits is data.** Components, variants, material zones, camera presets,
wheel anchors and fitment bounds all come from the asset manifest and part catalogue — there
are no per-vehicle branches in the UI.

### Data schemas (see `src/lib/schemas/index.ts`)

- **Vehicle** — year/make/model/trim, vehicle type, body/cab/bed style, dimensions, tags,
  attribution, `assetManifestId | null`, known limitations.
- **AssetManifest** — asset source + licence, scale/units/coordinate system, supported
  features, LODs, `meshNodes` (node name → component + material zone + explode offset),
  material zones, wheel anchors (with well clearances), camera targets/presets, fitment bounds.
- **Part / PartVariant** — category, mesh nodes, compatibility (vehicle ids/types/body
  styles/year range/socket), variants (mesh-swap, material-override, procedural-wheel, gltf),
  removability, provenance.
- **Build** — installed parts + variants, paint per zone, glass tint, front/rear wheel & tyre
  setup, stance, annotations, Titanforge records, camera state, versioned timestamps.
- **FabricationRecord** — workflow status, priority/assignee/process/material, dimensions +
  tolerances (mm), scan-required flag, orientation notes, quantity/cost/supplier, attachments,
  notes, and a `manufacturingValidated` flag that the app can never set to `true` from display
  geometry.

Example manifest: `docs/examples/tf100-asset-manifest.example.json` (the live source of truth
is `src/lib/catalog/tf100-manifest.ts`; tests verify the generated GLB contains every node it
names). Example Titanforge export: `docs/examples/tf100-titanforge-export.example.json`.

### Adding a vehicle

1. Obtain a rights-safe glTF 2.0 asset with **separately named meshes** (component editing is
   impossible with a monolithic mesh — the UI says so honestly).
2. Put the `.glb` under `public/assets/vehicles/`.
3. Write an `AssetManifest` mapping node names → components/material zones, wheel anchors,
   camera presets and fitment bounds; register it in `src/lib/catalog/index.ts`.
4. Add the `Vehicle` entry (with attribution + licence) to `src/lib/catalog/vehicles.ts` and
   its parts/variants to the catalogue.
5. Run the schema tests (`npm test`) — they validate all catalogue data.

### Adding a part/variant

Add a `Part` (mesh nodes, category, socket, compatibility) and its `PartVariant`s. Variant
visuals: `mesh-swap` (alternate nodes in the same GLB), `material-override` (e.g. painted vs
chrome bumper), `procedural-wheel` (parametric wheels), or `gltf` for external assets.

## Feature notes & honest limitations

- **Import**: PNG/JPEG/WebP reference images, glTF 2.0 (.glb/.gltf) and STL. Files are
  validated by **byte signature**, size caps and structural checks; OBJ/FBX/3MF are rejected
  with a conversion hint (server-side conversion is out of scope). Imported photos are
  references only, never "converted" to editable 3D. Imported 3D without a manifest loads as a
  monolithic preview (no per-part editing). Provenance + licence + reuse confirmation are
  mandatory before an asset enters the library. No scraping or URL extraction of protected
  assets.
- **Share links**: intentionally not offered — there is no server backend, and a fake link
  would lie. The Share dialog explains the truthful alternative (versioned build-file
  export/import). The repository interfaces in `src/lib/persistence/repositories.ts` are the
  seam where a real backend (auth, DB, object storage) plugs in.
- **Titanforge**: records live with the build; a local adapter implements the
  `TitanforgeAdapter` seam (`src/lib/titanforge`). No external Titanforge API exists or is
  faked. Exports (JSON/CSV) label every dimension as unvalidated; CSV output is
  formula-injection safe. Per-part geometry export is deliberately not enabled: the display
  meshes are not watertight or calibrated, and exporting them as "printable" would mislead.
- **Fitment warnings** (tyre clearance, poke, camber) are geometric estimates from manifest
  bounds and are labelled *indicative* everywhere they appear.
- **Persistence**: local-first IndexedDB with debounced autosave (visible status), multiple
  named builds/variants, exact restore after refresh, and versioned JSON export/import.
- **Accessibility/perf**: reduced-motion support (system preference + manual toggle, disables
  turntable/camera animation and switches to on-demand rendering), keyboard access with
  visible focus, labelled controls, per-node material disposal, lazy-loaded 3D code, and a
  viewer error boundary with a recovery path.

## Storage → production backend

The MVP binds `BuildRepository`, `AssetRepository` and `SettingsRepository` to IndexedDB.
To go multi-user: implement the same interfaces against your API (see `.env.example` for the
`VITE_BACKEND_URL` seam), keep IndexedDB as the offline cache, then enable share links in the
Share dialog once persisted server routes exist.

## Asset licensing requirements

Only supplied, licensed, public-domain or explicitly approved assets may be added. Every
manifest and import carries source, creator, licence and attribution text, and imports require
an explicit reuse confirmation. Catalogue vehicle names are factual metadata; no manufacturer
assets are bundled.
